theme: As a deer pants for flowing streams
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 42. It is the cry of a person who longs for God in a time of depression and exile. Pay attention to how the psalmist talks to his own soul.
settingTheScene: Psalm 42 opens Book II of the Psalter and is attributed to the sons of Korah. The psalmist is far from the temple, “from the land of Jordan and of Hermon,” in the far north. He is cut off from worship and surrounded by taunts. Placed here, at the beginning of the divided kingdom, it speaks for believers who feel the loss of the true worship of God. Psalms 42 and 43 are really one poem with a repeated refrain.
observation: “As a deer pants for flowing streams, so pants my soul for you, O God” (v. 1).
“My soul thirsts for God, for the living God. When shall I come and appear before God?” (v. 2).
“My tears have been my food day and night, while they say to me all the day long, Where is your God?” (v. 3).
“These things I remember, as I pour out my soul: how I would go with the throng and lead them in procession to the house of God” (v. 4).
“Why are you cast down, O my soul, and why are you in turmoil within me? Hope in God; for I shall again praise him, my salvation and my God” (v. 5).
“Deep calls to deep at the roar of your waterfalls; all your breakers and your waves have gone over me” (v. 7).
“By day the LORD commands his steadfast love, and at night his song is with me, a prayer to the God of my life” (v. 8).
“I say to God, my rock: Why have you forgotten me?” (v. 9).
interpretation:
The psalm begins with one of the most beautiful images in the Bible: a deer in a drought, panting for water. The word “pants” conveys urgency. The animal’s life depends on finding a stream. The psalmist’s soul feels the same need for God. It is not a mild interest in religion. It is a thirst that cannot be satisfied by anything else.

The cause of his pain is twofold. First, he is cut off from the community of worshipers. He remembers going with the crowd to the house of God, with shouts of joy and thanksgiving. Now it is only a memory. Second, he faces mockery: “Where is your God?” The question is cruel because the psalmist himself half wonders. In times of suffering, God’s absence feels real.

What the psalmist does next is crucial. He talks to himself. “Why are you cast down, O my soul?” He does not simply give in to his feelings. He questions them. He addresses his soul as a person to be instructed. And he gives it an instruction: “Hope in God.” The refrain appears three times in Psalms 42 and 43, as though the psalmist must say it over and over. Faith is sometimes a matter of preaching to oneself.

Verse 7 is one of the most haunting: “Deep calls to deep.” The waves of trouble come one after another, and he feels submerged. But even there, God has not left. “By day the LORD commands his steadfast love, and at night his song is with me.” In the midst of the flood, there is a song. The psalmist does not claim to feel better, but he affirms where hope lies.

He does not hide the hard question: “Why have you forgotten me?” Honest prayer includes honest questions. And he answers them not with explanations but with the refrain: “Hope in God.”
connection: Jesus said, “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John 7:37), and he promised the woman at the well living water (John 4:10-14). He experienced forsakenness on the cross for our sake (Matthew 27:46). Revelation 7:17 promises that the Lamb “will guide them to springs of living water.” Peter calls us to hope in God through Christ (1 Peter 1:21). Jesus himself said, “My soul is very sorrowful” (Matthew 26:38).
application:
Preach to yourself today. Take the refrain, “Hope in God,” and speak it to your soul.

Remember a time of joyful worship, and let it feed your longing.

Bring your honest question, “Why?” to God. Do not stop at the question; add the hope.
prayerPrompts: Tell God what your soul thirsts for.
Ask him to teach you to hope in him when you are cast down.
Ask him for his steadfast love by day and song by night.
